title: The angel in Nazareth (Luke 1:26–38)
hookLine: Gabriel greets a young woman in a small town, and she asks one honest question before saying yes

cards: A small town in the hills of Galilee: Nazareth. So ordinary that later in the Gospels someone asks whether anything good could come out of it. A young woman named Mary lives there, engaged to a man called Joseph.
One day, Luke says, the angel Gabriel comes in to where she is and greets her: hail, you who are highly favored, the Lord is with you. Mary is troubled.
She turns the words over in her mind, wondering what kind of greeting this could be. The angel says: don't be afraid. You're going to have a son, and you'll name him Jesus.
And Mary doesn't faint, and doesn't simply nod. She asks one question.

teach.b: Her question is practical: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" She's engaged, not married. Luke tells the answer plainly: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be called the Son of God.
And her older relative Elizabeth, the one people called barren, is six months pregnant. "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
Then Mary answers, and the week turns on this line: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." A question, and then a yes.
Not a yes without thinking; a yes after thinking. Luke never gives her age. Some readers picture a teenager, but the text doesn't say.
The scene's name is the annunciation, the announcement, and tradition keeps its feast on March twenty-fifth, nine months before Christmas.
Gabriel's first word in Greek is an everyday greeting that literally means rejoice.
The next words, highly favored, are one Greek word, which the old Latin Bible rendered full of grace.
Christians honor Mary in different ways, and this scene runs through them.

teach.h: BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.
teach.b: Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting. Orthodox Christians call her the Theotokos, the God-bearer, and sing to her often.
Protestants often honor her above all as a model of faith: someone who heard something impossible, asked her honest question, and said yes.

how: Churches keep the Annunciation as a feast on March 25; Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the Angelus, which retell this scene, Orthodox Christians sing hymns to Mary as Theotokos, and Protestant churches often read the passage in Advent.

games.q: you're Mary. an angel has just told you you'll have a son. what do you say first?
o: you ask how this can be.
games.why: she asks, "how shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" only after the answer does she say: "be it unto me according to thy word."

practice: Think of one small thing you've been hesitating over, not a life decision: a call you keep not making, an invitation you haven't answered, a favor someone asked for.
Do what Mary does in the story and ask your honest question first: what's the worry, really? Let it be said inside, and then, if it still seems good, say a quiet yes to it.

wordCard.voice: Annunciation. The announcement: an angel, a young woman's question, and her yes. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: rejoice, and an everyday hello. Gabriel's first word to Mary; the King James says hail.

carryVoice: Your line: be it unto me. Her yes came after her honest question. Day thirty-seven, done.
